new_statements.quote: En provisional conclusión se dirá que en el caso ibérico los diversos testimonios disponibles apuntan más bien a un tipo de acento demarcativo, más bien fijo y más bien final (oxítono) que inicial, al menos para un contingente importante y patrimonial de formas. Esa oxitonía en algunos casos habría quedado obscurecida por el hecho de que en las adaptaciones tanto griegas como latinas correspondía a una sílaba desinencial, de modo que esta habría sido adaptada en muchos casos. En cualquier caso y pace SILGO, no puede —nos parece— darse por segura una general acentuación paroxítona en ibérico.
new_statements.translation: By way of provisional conclusion it may be said that, in the Iberian case, the various available testimonies point rather to a demarcative type of accent, rather fixed and rather final (oxytone) than initial, at least for an important, native stock of forms. That oxytony would in some cases have been obscured by the fact that in both Greek and Latin adaptations it corresponded to an inflectional syllable, so that it would have been adapted in many cases. In any event, and pace Silgo, a general paroxytone accentuation in Iberian cannot — it seems to us — be taken as certain.
new_statements.citation: Ballester, Xaverio (2003). "El acento en la reconstrucción lingüística: el caso ibérico". Palaeohispanica 3: 43-57.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (15 pp., text layer; the PDF's metadata gives the title "El acento en la reconstrucción lingüística: el caso ibérico", Palaeohispanica 3 (2003), running heads pp. 43-57). PDF page 14 = printed p. 56, section "Conclusión": the quoted passage is there verbatim, from "En provisional conclusión se dirá que en el caso ibérico.." through "..pace SILGO, no puede —nos parece— darse por segura una general acentuación paroxítona en ibérico." I rendered the page to an image and checked it: the em-dashes and "pace SILGO" match the reader's quote exactly (extracted text renders the dashes as "²", an extraction artifact only). Also read pp. 47-55 (the "El caso del ibérico" section): p. 47 restates…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No direct evidence exists (script-only language). Two competing reconstructions: Ballester (2003) infers a fixed, demarcative, word-final (oxytone) accent from agglutinative typology, aspiration in URCHAIL, and Greek adaptations such as Saitabí; Silgo (1994-95: 185) infers from Old Basque accent, syncope (beleś > bels) and surviving toponyms an intensity accent that 'in most cases fell on the second syllable counting from the end' (penultimate), with initial accent attractive for the mostly bisyllabic segments. The field has not settled the question.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed for Iberian in either source.
new_statements.exceptions: Ballester: oxytony masked in Latin/Greek adaptations (Latin cannot have oxytones; forms with closed penult such as iltiŕta are forced paroxytone in Latin; Latin Baetulo, Barcino, Ilici, Tarraco are antepenult by Latin rule). Silgo (p. 185): compounds of two bisyllabic elements stressed on the first syllable of the second element (Estavar, Barguja, i.e. third syllable); atonic suffixes and accent-attracting suffixes; 'irregularities' like *biós ~ Basque bihótz; explicit 'cierta falta de uniformidad'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical accent, reconstructed for an extinct language with no phonetic record; evidence is onomastic (toponyms of the Valencian/Catalan area, anthroponyms in Latin inscriptions, Greek/Latin adaptations). Both authors treat it as a fixed word accent; Ballester frames it as a demarcative accent typical of agglutinative languages.
new_statements.identity_note: Iberian proper (iber1250 / xib), the language of the Palaeohispanic north-eastern and Levantine scripts, extinct since c. 1st c. AD. Both sources treat the language as a whole; the toponymic evidence comes from the Valencian region and north-west Catalonia. Not to be confused with Celtiberian or Tartessian/South-western.

new_statements.quote: En efecto, recientemente nos hemos ocupado de la posición del acento en ibérico y antes, en un trabajo presentado en el último Coloquio de lenguas y culturas arqueoibéricas, del estatuto fonemático de las consonantes continuas. [p. 362] ... En esa circunstancia diversos factores, como, por ejemplo, la probable diferencia en la posición del acento (/tarakón/ ~ /tárrakoo/), la inexistencia de vocales largas en ibérico o la existencia de geminadas en latín obligaban o al menos invitaban a un reajuste para mantener equilibradas las correspondencias más esenciales permitiendo así un registro como Tarraco para TaRACoN. [p. 363]
new_statements.translation: Indeed, we have recently dealt with the position of the accent in Iberian and, earlier, in a paper presented at the last Colloquium on archaeo-Iberian languages and cultures, with the phonemic status of the continuant consonants. [p. 362] ... In that circumstance various factors, such as, for example, the probable difference in the position of the accent (/tarakón/ ~ /tárrakoo/), the non-existence of long vowels in Iberian or the existence of geminates in Latin forced or at least invited a readjustment to keep the most essential correspondences balanced, thus allowing a rendering like Tarraco for TaRACoN. [p. 363]

(b) p. 363: 'En esa circunstancia diversos factores, como, por ejemplo, la probable diferencia en la…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the existing Ballester 2003 statement (demarcative, rather fixed, rather final/oxytone accent): the single transcribed example /tarakón/ vs Latin /tárrakoo/ illustrates final stress in an Iberian word, but the 2005 paper only presupposes the 2003 result and adds no independent argument. It says nothing about Silgo's penultimate reconstruction. The catalog record itself has an empty rule, so this neither confirms nor contradicts a catalog placement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: The article is about rhotics and ergativity and has no stress section. It mentions stress only incidentally: it refers back to the author's 2003 study of Iberian accent position, and it transcribes the Iberian toponym TaRACoN as /tarakón/ (final stress) against Latin /tárrakoo/, calling the difference in accent position 'probable'. That is consistent with the oxytone (final, demarcative) reconstruction Ballester argued in 2003, but the 2005 paper gives no rule of its own.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the paper also states Iberian had no long vowels and no geminates except perhaps /n/ (p. 364), which bears on weight but not on stress placement
new_statements.identity_note: Ballester 2005 treats Iberian proper (epigraphic forms in the Levantine script, e.g. TaRACoN, BaRCeNO, USECeŘTe; MLH references), not Celtiberian, Tartessian or Basque. The same volume contains Lakarra's article on Proto-Basque accent (pp. 407-470), which is about Basque and was not used.

readall_conflicts: The two substantive reconstructions held by the project disagree and Ballester 2005 does not resolve them: Silgo 1994-95 (Arse 28-29: 185) reconstructs an intensity accent falling in most cases on the penultimate syllable, whereas Ballester 2003 (Palaeohispanica 3: 56) argues for a demarcative, rather fixed, rather final (oxytone) accent and explicitly says a general paroxytone accentuation cannot be taken as certain. Ballester 2005 only presupposes his own 2003 oxytone view in one transcribed example (/tarakón/) and gives no new evidence, so the conflict between penultimate (Silgo) and final (Ballester) stands. Stress in Iberian is a reconstruction from Latin/Greek adaptations and internal syncope patterns, not an observation.

sources.note: Whole article is on Iberian accent reconstruction. Argues from agglutinative typology (fixed, peripheral demarcative accent expected), aspiration (URCHAIL -> oxytone [urkh'ajl]), vowel behaviour, and Greek/Latin adaptations (Latin cannot show oxytones; Greek Saitabí for śaitabi) that Iberian accent was 'demarcativo, más bien fijo y más bien final (oxítono) que inicial'; rejects Silgo's general paroxytony as unproven (pp. 47, 54-56).

sources.citation: Silgo Gauche, Luis (1994-1995). "Algunos datos sobre el acento ibérico". Arse 28-29: 175-185 (Dialnet: 175-186). Sagunto: Centro Arqueológico Saguntino.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Reconstructs Iberian accent from Old Basque accent (Michelena), syncope (beleś > bels) and pre-Roman toponyms of Valencia/Catalonia. Conclusion p. 185: accent 'de intensidad y columnal', initial accent attractive for the mostly bisyllabic segments, but longer toponyms show it 'caía en la mayoría de los casos sobre la segunda sílaba contando desde el final' (penultimate); atonic and accent-attracting suffixes; compounds stressed on first syllable of second element; admits lack of uniformity.
